✨ But we provide links to helpful AI-generated content along the way.
:::

AI is radically redefining the nature of scientific inquiry — for better and for worse. 

In Fall 2026, faculty, graduate students, and postdocs across multiple departments at the University of Florida came together to understand this urgent development. In a seminar titled *Collective [Artificial] Intelligence in Science*, we documented and discussed how AI is changing each component of our research workflow. This includes project management, idea development, data analysis, writing, and dissemination. To push our understanding, we alternated between the perspectives of an AI zealot and an AI critic — identifying key resources, consensus statements, and areas of disagreement along the way. The result is the **2027 UF Guide to AI in Science**.

The seminar began with an introduction to big-team science — its rise[@Coles2022], competitive advantages[@Coles2026], and relevance to the current moment. For instance, the paper describing OpenAI’s GPT-1 had 4 authors[@radford2018improving]; the paper describing GPT-3 had 31 authors[@brown2020language]; and the paper describing GPT-5 had 483 authors[@openai2025gpt5] (@fig-scale-ladder). Similarly, a prominent AI-led cybersecurity attack on the online community, Hugging Face, involved coordinated action among not one but *thousands* of AI agents[@openai2026huggingface].

```{r}
#| label: fig-scale-ladder

#| fig-width: 7.5

scale_ladder_plot(fig_width = 7.5)
```


After reviewing these developments, the course itself became a large-scale collaboration, dedicated to understanding how AI is changing the nature of science. Each week followed a consistent structure (@fig-seminar-structure). First, we would select a component of the research pipeline to examine (e.g., data analysis). Second, we would spend one week compiling resources for understanding the emerging role of AI in that part of the research pipeline. Third, we would engage in peer-to-peer teaching. Last, we would use a live online voting platform to solicit, debate, and vote upon key resources and takeaways for the week[@Coles2024; @dalkey1963delphi]. Through these exercises, seminar participants received hands on experience with large-scale collaboration[@Baumgartner2023; @nrc2015team]. Along the way, not only developed and debated their *personal* philosophy statements -- but also the general direction of AI at UF. Their results culminate into this **2027 UF Guide to AI in Science**: a summary of our top resources, takeaways, and disagreements.
